newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spotlight turns on Kohl and Prodi after EMU report.
newsitem.headline: Spotlight turns on Kohl and Prodi after EMU report.

text.p: Reports on Wednesday of a European Union plan to delay Italian entry into the bloc's new single currency intensified the spotlight on a summit between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Analysts said if the reports were true, one of Kohl's main tasks at Friday's Bonn summit would be to convince Prodi to continue on the path of fiscal discipline by offering assurance that Rome could join soon after the currency's launch in 1999.
"This is now the difficulty -- how to tell the Italians without losing their faith," said Eckhard Schulte, an economist at Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt.

Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Julius Baer in Frankfurt, said the plan was no surprise, bearing in mind strong German reservations about the credibility of the euro if it included a traditionally soft currency like the lira from the start.
"The problem here is that Prodi going to have to explain this to his own people," he said.

EU officials confirmed a report in Wednesday's Financial Times, which said Italy would be offered the chance to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 2000 or 2001, partly to assuage German fears of a soft euro.
Under the scheme, a "hard core" of EU members would press ahead with EMU in 1999, the paper said.

Italy, Spain and Portugal -- the countries often dubbed with the slightly derogatory term "Club Med" -- all denied knowledge of such a plan, as did German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and a French government source.
But financial market and economists said there was sufficient unofficial confirmation to convince them that there was some truth to the report.

German government sources said there had been no political talks on a plan but added bureaucrats may have discussed the idea. Bonn officials have hinted before that currencies without a history of stability should not be founding EMU members.

Prodi issued a statement deploring "the constant repetition of false stories... which have no foundation whatsoever" -- but he acknowledged only last month that German hostility to Italian initial EMU membership was a problem.

The Financial Times said the plan, being formulated by European central bankers and monetary officials, could be extended to other southern European countries -- the so-called Club Med members of the EU.

Kohl, who met another Club Med hopeful last week in the form of Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, will hold more than three hours of talks with Prodi and other Italian ministers during Friday's summit at the Bonn chancellery.
The two leaders are scheduled to hold a joint news conference after the talks.
The veteran chancellor, widely seen as the driving force behind European integration, said on Tuesday he would tell Prodi both Italy and Germany still had work to do on the road to EMU.
"Our Italian friends have the same problems as the Germans. They must do their homework," he told reporters in Berlin. "I'll tell my friend my Prodi that you'll have to do your homework. We do too."
Economists said there was a danger that any plan to exclude Italy from the founding members of EMU could prompt Rome to stray from its course of financial austerity.

"I see the risk that they say we haven't managed it, all our efforts have come to nothing, we'll let up again' and that risk must be overcome by offering a perspective (for entry)," a senior economist at one major Frankfurt bank said. The economist, who asked not to be named, said the risk was "not small", but Grebe at Julius Baer said political and economic arguments would lead Italy to stick with its current course, even if it had to wait a little longer than it had hoped.

"Italy is very Europe-friendly and has always belonged to those countries which pushed forward European integration," he said. "I think also that the currency union is attractive enough that Italy will simply want to be a part of it."
